$comment: The claims ladder of proofs/README.md, declared as DATA so a registry can read it
rather than parse prose. Hand-authored and never generated: the point of the manifest is
that a human decided which rung each claim sits on, and a generator would only be able to
restate what the code already says.
`level` is a CLOSED set — proved | tested | assumed | policy — and the four map onto the
README's four rungs: proved, differentially tested, assumed-and-stated, and not-claimed.
A `policy` entry is an exclusion carrying its reason, because an unstated exclusion reads,
to whoever finds it later, as a claim that failed.
A `proved` entry names its lemma and the prover pin so an evidence check can resolve the
lemma in the named module and the pin in the named file. Nothing here is checkable by
reading this file alone, and that is the intended shape: the manifest says where to look,
the proof leg (proofs/check.ps1) is what looks.
Every later proof phase in this repository appends its claims here rather than starting a
Phase 790 appended the disclosure-fold claims (ids prefixed `disclosure-`); the five headline
lemmas are one `proved` entry each, so an evidence check resolves them by name.
Phase 793 appended the tool-gate claims (ids prefixed `toolgate-`): the four lemmas, the
differential host, the two opaque authority predicates, and the policy entries that say what the
envelope does not bind and where the approval-by-class keying is decided.
subject: the proved models under proofs/: ToolUp.Remoting.Decode - the combinator algebra over the closed MessagePack value model (Phase 787); the disclosure algebra - DisclosureEgress.evaluate plus the population fold PopulationDisclosure.fold / valuesWithheld / disclosedStats (Phase 790); and the AI tool gate - ToolGate.decideDeclared, AIToolRegistry.ListAccessible and the dispatch-site re-check over the declared ToolEffect class (Phase 793)

fstar-pinned.reproducibility: proof hints no longer exist in this prover, so the pin, a margin on --z3rlimit, and --quake 3 over three cold runs are what stand in for them

claims.statement: Given a parsed value, no combinator and no decoder built from them can diverge, throw, or reach a state that is neither an accept nor a named refusal. Quantified over ALL decoders, not one lemma per combinator, so it covers anything a consumer or a generator composes out of the algebra.
Which outcome, for which input, with the exact refusal - expected text, found text and path. The failure classification is exhaustive rather than merely non-empty.

The element accessor that both the positional-field and the index combinator are built from returns a value strictly smaller than its input, by the value model's own size measure. A decoder descending through it cannot recur forever, and not because of a depth counter.

evidence.note: carried in element_at's REFINED RETURN TYPE, so every descent consumes it at the call site

claims.statement: The integer width rule is about INFORMATION, not signed range: a negative value never decodes into an unsigned target and fits a signed target exactly when it clears its minimum; a source no wider than its target always survives, sign reinterpretation included; a source wider than its target must fit its range; and the rule decides for every width class.

On a reader-producible value, an Int32 accept implies the payload carries no more than thirty-two bits of information - the union of the signed and unsigned 32-bit ranges. It deliberately does NOT imply the payload sits in Int32's signed range, because a negative decimal word arrives unsigned and the host's cast reinterprets it. That union is exactly the set on which the cast is a bijection.

evidence.premise: value_wf - the payload is within the width class its format byte declared. The one-pass reader produces only such values by construction; see the assumption `well-formedness-not-enforced-by-type`.

claims.statement: Over a reference API-record vocabulary - a nested record with a string, a bounded integer and a flag - the encoding of any value decodes, and decodes back to the value it started from. Not merely 'decodes to something': the decoder can never refuse traffic its own encoder produced.

The extracted model and the shipped algebra decode every covered wire-corpus case and every refuse-path mutation to the same outcome class, the same value, the same runtime type and the same refusal message. This is the only thing that says the proved model is about the code that runs.

cases: the extracted model agrees with production over every covered corpus case
the extracted model agrees with production over every refuse-path mutation
the model never throws, on any corpus payload, at any covered type
the reference vocabulary round-trips through the extracted encoder and decoder

claims.statement: The committed oracle is byte-identical to a fresh extraction from the checked module. Without this the committed file would be a claim; with it, a checked one.

A committed go-red case hands the model a bridge that has forgotten the source width class, and asserts the comparison catches it. It catches four cases and every one is the width rule losing. A differential never shown to fail agrees with whatever it is shown.

cases: the differential CATCHES a bridge that forgets the source width - the go-red case
and the width rule is what it catches

claims.statement: The extractor and the F# compiler are trusted. The theorem is about the model; the code that runs is the extraction, and nothing verifies that the extraction preserves semantics.
claims.mitigation: the differential host runs the EXTRACTION, not the model, so an extraction defect that changes behaviour on any corpus payload is caught there

claims.statement: The value-to-model bridge in the differential host is hand-written. A defect in it would make the comparison compare the wrong thing.
claims.mitigation: short and case-for-case on purpose, and the committed go-red bridge beside it exercises the one field most likely to be got wrong

claims.statement: The extractor's F# backend ships no runtime, so the nine names it references are supplied by a hand-written shim.
claims.mitigation: small enough to read in a minute; the byte-diff means a model change reaching for a tenth name fails the leg rather than compiling against a widened shim

claims.statement: Three payload facts come from the host rather than the model: a string's length, a binary payload's length, and a float's rendered text. Recomputing any of them would introduce a second implementation free to disagree with the host's - and for string length it demonstrably would, the two runtimes counting different units.
claims.mitigation: carried as data on the value model, so the model's refusals quote the host's own numbers

claims.statement: The value model admits an integer whose payload exceeds its declared width class. The one-pass reader cannot produce one, but nothing here enforces it.
claims.mitigation: the lemmas that need it carry it as an explicit premise rather than assuming it away

claims.statement: Proof hints were removed from this prover, so the usual way to pin an SMT search is unavailable. The pinned release and its bundled solver, a margin on the resource limit, and three cold runs under --quake 3 are evidence of stability, not a guarantee of it.
The bytes-to-value pass is OUT of the theorem.
claims.reason: it is bounded - length against remaining on every length-prefixed read, and a depth ceiling - but bounded is not proved. This is the one place a binary-format proof framework would apply if it is ever wanted. A payload the reader itself refuses never reaches either decoder, and the differential skips it rather than pretending otherwise.

claims.statement: The System.Text.Json decode path is OUT.
claims.reason: its value carrier is undecided - the current JSON value model's numeric case cannot carry a 64-bit integer past 2^53, an exact decimal, or the source width

claims.statement: The reflection decode path is OUT, by construction rather than by omission.
claims.reason: it is an interpreter over an open, possibly recursive type graph walked with a mutable cursor, so 'total on every input' is not a well-formed statement about it - the input includes the type graph. That asymmetry is the whole argument for the closed value model.

claims.statement: One narrowing is unrefusable at the decoder.
claims.reason: the writer compacts a 64-bit value into bytes that ARE a well-formed 32-bit one - the shape a decimal's sign word travels in. The value model faithfully carries a 32-bit source and the information rule admits it, correctly, since refusing it would refuse every negative decimal the corpus pins. Closing it needs a writer that never compacts across a sign boundary, which is a wire break.

claims.statement: A trailing element past a record's declared fields is accepted, not refused.
claims.reason: a record decoder reads the positions it declares and ignores what follows, in agreement with the reflection reader. That is what keeps an additive wire change non-breaking, and it is the one evolution property this wire has.

claims.statement: A decoded value is well-typed. It is not authorised, not tenant-scoped and not semantically valid.
claims.reason: those are other boundaries' obligations; a decode theorem that implied them would be claiming something it cannot see

claims.statement: The date-only and time-only primitives have no combinator, so no model.
claims.reason: one of the two hosts' readers refuses both types outright, so a primitive for them would decode on one host and not the other. This ships a cross-host algebra or it ships nothing.

claims.statement: A record still decoding through the reflection path is outside every claim above.
claims.reason: the algebra is an opt-in replacement for a decoder that already works; the shipped default is unchanged

claims.statement: For any ranking, any total verdict function and any policy assignment, no fact whose verdict is not-disclosable appears in the disclosed list.

The withheld count and the withheld projection are functions of the verdict list alone - the count is the number of not-disclosable verdicts and the projection is countBy-then-sortBy over their policy refs. The relational corollary states it over two rankings whose facts may differ in every field and even in TYPE: pointwise-equal verdicts give an identical projection, so no withheld fact's identity, rank or value was consulted.
Every disclosed (rank, fact) has fact at one-based position rank of the input ranking. A withheld member leaves a gap; a contiguous renumbering cannot satisfy this.

When anything was withheld, the gated summary's minimum, maximum and mean are absent; when nothing was, the summary is returned untouched; the existence-level fields ride through in both cases; and the gate fires exactly when some verdict denied. The biconditional is over the gate's ACTION - it does not say an absent magnitude implies a withheld member, since a summary over nothing comparable carries none to begin with.

Two rankings that agree on every disclosable fact and on every verdict yield IDENTICAL PopulationDisclosure records - the same disclosed list, the same withheld count, the same withheld projection - whatever the withheld facts' identities or values. No observation of the fold's output distinguishes one withheld population from another.

Which verdict, for which classification: Surfaceable is always disclosable, Internal never (naming the classification as its policy ref), and Restricted exactly when the resolver answers Some true - Some false and None both deny, so an unknown policy ref can never fail open. The conservative default denies every Restricted fact at every surface.

evidence.note: supporting, not one of the five: it is what ties the verdicts the fold consumes to the predicate that produces them

claims.statement: The extracted model and the shipped fold agree, on every ranking the three door packs pin (reproduced as data) and on 400 generated rankings with generated verdicts, on the disclosed list, the withheld projection and the gated summary AT ONCE; and the extracted predicate agrees with the shipped one over every classification, resolver and surface. This is the only thing that says the proved model is about the code that runs.

the extracted fold agrees with production over every suite ranking
the extracted fold agrees with production over generated rankings with generated verdicts

claims.statement: The committed oracle is byte-identical to a fresh extraction from the checked module.

A committed go-red oracle renumbers the disclosed ranks contiguously - the tidy-looking mistake that reports the third-best as the second-best - and the comparison is asserted to catch it, with the mechanism pinned on a three-member ranking (true ranks 1 and 3 against the oracle's 1 and 2). A differential never shown to fail agrees with whatever it is shown.

cases: the differential CATCHES an oracle that renumbers ranks contiguously - the go-red case
and the true-rank gap is what it catches

claims.statement: The theorem is about the FOLD, and the fold gates a summary the store computed over the WHOLE matched population. A restricted member ranked below the ceiling still contributed to that summary's Mean, and under a highest-first ranking can BE its Minimum. What is proved is that the gate acts on the summary exactly when it acts on the members; what is NOT proved, or claimed, is that a magnitude the gate lets through carries no information about a member the caller was never returned. The shipped code calls this a floor, not a proof, and so does this entry.
claims.mitigation: when ANY member of the ranking is withheld the whole magnitude block goes, so the residual is confined to members outside the ranking the caller asked for; a whole-population disclosure probe is a different capability

claims.statement: The ordering List.sortBy fst sorts the withheld projection by is host-supplied to the model as a before: string -> string -> bool, because F* has no string comparison that extracts to Prims alone. Every lemma holds for ANY ordering; what the model does not verify is that the host's ordinal comparison is the one the shipped code uses.
claims.mitigation: the differential compares the projection's ORDER as part of the withheld projection, so a host ordering that disagreed with List.sortBy would fail the leg on any ranking withheld under two policies

claims.statement: The Fact-to-model and PopulationStats-to-model bridges in the differential host are hand-written. A defect in either would make the comparison compare the wrong thing.
claims.mitigation: short and case-for-case on purpose: a fact is its id plus itself as the opaque payload, a summary is its three magnitudes plus itself as the opaque existence-level rest, so the read-back is a structural comparison of production's own records

claims.statement: That every door CALLS disclosedStats before reporting a summary is OUT of the theorem.
claims.reason: the theorem is about what the fold computes, not about who calls it; a summary type does not force the call, and the obligation is stated on the not-claimed rung of proofs/README.md, where the door packs are named as the evidence that the two shipped doors do

claims.statement: Statistical disclosure control is OUT. The theorem says nothing about what a determined reader could infer from a count, a period range or a freshness histogram, nor from the magnitudes of a ranking with nothing withheld.
claims.reason: the disclosure vocabulary is a declared classification enforced at egress, not an inference-control regime, and the shipped code's honesty boundary says so in the same words

claims.statement: For any RBAC predicate, any grant-liveness predicate, any ToolPolicy and any registry, no tool whose declared effects exceed the policy's ceiling is listed: under a bounded ceiling every listed tool's every declared effect has a class the ceiling names, and an undeclared tool is listed only when the policy admits undeclared tools. The supporting equality says an admitting verdict is EXACTLY the two authority predicates answering yes and the declaration sitting within the ceiling.

A tool is in the list exactly when it is in the registry and the decision admits it. Nothing the decision refused reaches the list, and nothing it admits is dropped - the list filter and the decision are one function, not two that happen to agree.

If the dispatch-site re-check admits the name the model produced - looked up by authored name or provider alias, then decided - the list the model was offered carries a tool of that name. A forged, hallucinated or replayed name the list would have refused is refused at dispatch too. This is the 'two gates that must agree share their whole decision' comment on ListAccessible, as a lemma.

A tool declaring Egress to any destination is refused under every bounded ceiling that does not name the egress class, whatever else it declares and whatever the two authority predicates answer. This is the go-red property in proof form: a gate that dropped Egress before deciding would violate it.

The extracted model and the shipped gate agree on the VERDICT for every in-tree tool the host can reach (the narrative and cross-module built-ins, the three fact tools, the sample client tool) and for 60 generated tools, under 28 generated policies including the external-principal view of each, 11 generated callers and their grant predicates; on the LISTED SET, in order, under every policy and caller; and on the DISPATCH answer by authored name, by provider alias and for an unknown name. This is the only thing that says the proved model is about the code that runs.

claims.statement: The committed oracle is byte-identical to a fresh extraction from the checked module.

A committed go-red gate drops Egress from a declaration before deciding - measuring a tool by what it reads rather than where it reaches - and the comparison is asserted to catch it, with the mechanism pinned on one tool declaring only Egress under the read-only policy: production and the honest oracle refuse naming the egress, the blind gate admits. A differential never shown to fail agrees with whatever it is shown.

cases: the differential CATCHES a gate that ignores Egress - the go-red case
and egress under a read-only ceiling is what it catches

claims.statement: RBAC (isToolSourcePermittedFor over the caller's permission map, its Read/Write/Admin hierarchy and the SDK-reserved-namespace exemption) and grant liveness (moduleGrantGate over the request's consent stamps) are host-supplied predicates the model takes as total arrows. Every lemma holds for any pair; what the model does not verify is what either answers. They are earlier phases' decisions, and modelling them would introduce a second implementation free to disagree with the host's.
claims.mitigation: the differential host passes production's own isToolSourcePermittedFor and generated grant predicates to BOTH sides, so the verdicts compared include the two refusals those predicates produce

claims.statement: The bridge from the shipped types to the model's is hand-written: an effect case for case, a declared set as its sorted list, a policy's ceiling and undeclared flag, a registered tool's name, alias, source and folded declaration. A defect in it would make the comparison compare the wrong thing.
claims.mitigation: short and case-for-case on purpose; the go-red gate beside it is built from production's OWN decision over a perturbed declaration, so the comparison is known to see a declaration defect

claims.statement: The effect envelope refuses what a DECLARED tool body reaches for through the SDK's seams - a host capability through ToolEffectEnvelope.guardInvoke, an outbound request through guardEgress, a scoped write through guardWrite. An executor that constructs its own HttpClient, opens a socket or writes a file directly is outside every check, exactly as it is outside the composition capability gate. Nothing short of process-level isolation closes that, and nothing here claims to.
claims.mitigation: the verified composition profile makes the declaration mandatory, so under it every in-tree tool is bound at the seams; a tool's own outbound call is the one place an author must route through guardEgress, and the envelope test pack pins that a ReadFacts tool cannot send through it

claims.statement: The policy ceiling is expressed over effect CLASSES, with payloads erased; a ceiling cannot say 'egress to api.example.com but nowhere else'.
claims.reason: a ceiling that could only name exact destinations or scopes could never say 'no egress at all', which is the sentence a policy most needs to say; the exact payload is checked at the moment of use by the envelope, which refuses Egress 'b' under a declaration of Egress 'a'

claims.statement: The human-in-the-loop approval hold is keyed on effect class through ToolPolicy.RequireApproval and ToolApprovalDispatch.requirementByClass, in FRONT of the deployment's own IToolApprovalPolicy: a tool declaring a held class is held whatever that policy says about it by name, and a tool declaring none falls through to it unchanged.
claims.reason: a per-tool name list widens silently the moment a module registers a new tool; a class-keyed hold binds the new tool by what it declares. The composition and its rationale are in docs/migrations/793-tool-effect-class.md and docs/ai/extending.md; the external-principal ceiling (ToolPolicy.ExternalPrincipalCeiling) is the same keying applied to an agent's grants, default-deny by class

claims.statement: A client-resident tool's body runs in the browser and is OUT of the envelope.
claims.reason: the envelope is an ambient server-side value around Execute, and a client-resident dispatch never calls Execute; the browser-side body is bound by the client-tool allowlist seam instead, and the gate's list and dispatch decisions apply to both locations alike
